newsitem.title: HONG KONG: IPO VIEW - Hong Kong IPOs flow seen slowing in April.
newsitem.headline: IPO VIEW - Hong Kong IPOs flow seen slowing in April.

text.p: Hong Kong may see a slowdown in new share offers this month because of weak sentiment, competition from H-share results and a new attention to approvals from Chinese authorities, analysts said.

"Sentiment certainly will affect the pace of listing," said Andrew Kuet, an analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell, adding that fears of higher interest rates were causing investors to be more cautious in the U.S. and local stock markets.
The Hang Seng Index has fallen nearly 1,200 points since the beginning of March to close at 12,204.59 on Friday.

So far only two locally based companies -- switch and socket maker Wing Lee Holdings Ltd and Pacific Ports Co Ltd, a spin-off from Fairyoung Holdings Ltd -- have announced initial public offering (IPO) plans for April.
This compares to nine companies listed in March and a total of 19 companies floated in the first quarter of 1997.
"Some merchant bankers may advise their clients to rediscuss the P/E (price earnings) level of their shares due to the recent market trend," said Sean Li, associate director at Amsteel Securities.

But he also said market condition was unpredictable, and April was generally a quiet month for IPOs since the fiscal years for some companies had just begun and this might affect the auditing process.

"A number of companies planned to list their shares in April, but somehow no more news was heard from them and they probably could not make it this month," said one account manager at a public relations company.

Market sources said some China-play listing candidates did not want to compete with H-shares for attention as the reporting season for the Hong Kong-listed China-incorporated companies kicks off next week.
"Starting a roadshow in April is really a bad timing," said an executive at an international public relation agency.
"We recommend our clients do not fight for attention in April since a string of H-shares companies are planning overseas presentations following their result announcements," he said.
Market sources said a number of mainland China companies were queuing up for a Hong Kong listing, with at least six aiming for a public offering in the first half of 1997.

But talk that last month's listing by China-play GITIC Enterprises Ltd had almost foundered due to a failure to obtain prior approvals from Chinese authorities had left the securities industry confused, market sources added.
They said it was unclear whether Hong Kong-based companies controlled by mainland Chinese parents, such as GITIC Enterprises, needed approval from Chinese authorities.
But some may be asking for it anyway, delaying the listing process, they said.

Market sources said one such company that may have to list at a later date than initially expected was Chaozhou Industries Ltd, the eel farm unit of Guangnan (Holdings) Ltd, which had aimed to float in early 1997.
Sources said they had expected Chaozhou to offer 125 million shares at HK$1.0-1.10 with dealing beginning on April 15.
But they said the company was now unlikely to meet that date and there were rumours it was awaiting approval from the China Securities Regulatory Commission.
An executive at one of the arrangers said details of the issue had not been finalised. "Once the issue has been finalised or there is any progress, we will make an announcement," she said.
